abstract.p: The speaker addresses the townsmen of Oxford, accusing them of being too foolish and insensitive to properly grieve their dead mayor. He says they lack judgment, don’t understand true sorrow, and probably wouldn’t mourn anyone worthy. Davenant is presented as a competent and moderating figure who kept order in the town, protected it from ridicule, and maintained a balance between the town and the university. Now that he’s dead, the townspeople are exposed again to mockery (especially from scholars) and their incompetence will become obvious.

div.head:
On Mr John Davnant Who died on Thursday
Aprill the 18. 1622 being thee Maior of Oxford.
Dedicated to the Worthlesse and Wittlesse Townsmen

lg.l: Kinde Towne Freindes had I witt enough to sweare
Your little judgments knew what goodnesse were,
And so trew sorrow to you as unknowne,
As you have few dy that deservs our moone moan ;
I would not stirr your Lazy greife nor preach
Old Welladaies and woes beyond your reach:
Nor with fagg ends of doctrine you exhorte
To worke out teares amixt your Hollidaies sport.
But since your much suspected ignorance
I judgd unwitting, what a blow this chance
Hath given your corporation; and Davnant deade,
Leaft you unactive members without Head:
List well what cause of sorrow my Muse beares,
The Civill Heads gone, but hath left you the Eares.
You have lost a Maior who whylst you might him call
yours by his owne discretion eas’d you all
Of your deserved absurdeties; none stirrd
A Toungue against Towne-Government: no word
Against officers unlanguag’d that scarse know
A wise worde to speake, but speake good Master Snow.
Schollers could not bee witty, but when th’assay
To jest att you, Davnant stood in theire way,
And made them downe theire pens; For Whylst Hee bore
Th’office no councells held yee as before
To bearde the Accademy as earst yee durst,
Nor sought wether Ned the Fourth or third raigned first.
To find the oldest priviledge; neither bore
your Maiors such Envy to make Magdalens poore.
Oh ‘twere unthankefull rashly to putt downe
And begger Colledges that enrich the towne!
Now your deliverer that sett you free
From Bobbs and Pasquills (o hard desteny
To you not him!) by death is freed from paine,
And you lie ‘ope to Scholler witts againe.
Now I would wish you howle, else wee shall deeme
Your grossnese held not Davnant in esteeme
Worth Him, and there begines a quarrell just
To Raile, and therefore howle; indeed you must,
your judgments will be question’d else, and you thought
To feede no more then what goes downe your throate.
I’de say more to you but that my greife would show
Antike mock’te greife, and ill apparelld woe
If you suppose Davnants a common beare bier
Or greive in fashion, and no bloudye teare
Reserv’d only for Him bee shed, for Him
Only, whose compleate worth did others dimme;
If yee can not plucke upp one grone or sigh:
That growes neare to the heart, and to a height
Screw upp your sorrow dy yee and for your sakes
Your dull succession shall spend wine and Cakes,
And mourne as you for him: Whylst worthy hee
To be bemon’d of better spirits, shall bee
Scholarlike greiv’d for and theire watry eies
Shall wash theire stubborne sinne. Do not dispise
This seasonable motion worthy yee
That weere wear Minerva’s livery; only Hee
Only hee was capable to bee bemon’d by you,
And thus distinguisht from the common crew
Of dying Townsmen: For His worthy parts
Spake Him part scholler, and neare to the Artes.
Nor shall this act breed custome noone beside
Shall flow your teares unto so high a tide.

div.head: Historical context and dating
div.p: John Davenant (1565–1622), vintner and proprietor of the Crown Inn, Cornmarket Street, Oxford was elected mayor on 17 September 1621. The Davenants were well-known, they kept an important inn frequented by Shakespeare, and their son William became a prominent dramatist.
